prompt: What does a story point measure?

choices.text: Risk of the story
choices.why: Risk may affect size, but points are not a risk score.

choices.text: Size relative to other work
choices.why: Right. Not hours, not days, not one person's effort.

choices.text: Hours of work for an average developer
choices.why: Points are deliberately not time.

choices.text: Value to the business
choices.why: Value is ordered by the Product Owner, separately.

prompt: A team loses a developer for a month. What happens to the size in points of a story it already estimated at 5?

choices.text: It stays 5; velocity drops instead
choices.why: Right. Relative size separates the work from the speed of the team.

choices.text: It falls to keep the velocity steady
choices.why: That would be inflating velocity's opposite: gaming.

choices.text: It rises, since fewer people will do it
choices.why: Size does not depend on who does the work.

choices.text: It must be re-estimated in hours
choices.why: No conversion is needed.

prompt: Why does the scale jump from 13 to 20 instead of going 13, 14, 15?

choices.text: Big items resist fine sizing
choices.why: Right. The gaps refuse a distinction nobody can make.

choices.text: The cards would not fit in a deck
choices.why: A deck could hold them; the gaps are deliberate.

choices.text: Fibonacci numbers are easier to add
choices.why: Ease of adding is not the reason.

choices.text: Scrum requires that exact scale
choices.why: Scrum prescribes no estimation scale.

prompt: Put a round of planning poker in order.
items: The Product Owner reads the story
trap: Choosing privately comes before the reveal; explaining comes after it.

prompt: Why are the cards revealed at the same moment?

choices.text: To make the meeting shorter
choices.why: The point is independence, not speed.

choices.text: So the Product Owner can count the votes
choices.why: Counting is not why the reveal is simultaneous.

choices.text: To avoid anchoring on the first number heard
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the first speaker's estimate becomes everybody's.

choices.text: Because the senior developer votes last
choices.why: Nobody votes last; that is the point.

prompt: One developer shows 3 and another 13. What should the team do, by the lesson?

choices.text: Hear why, then vote again
choices.why: Right. One of them knows something the other does not.

choices.text: Skip the story until next Sprint, since the team cannot agree
choices.why: Disagreement is resolved by discussion, not postponement.

choices.text: Take the average, 8
choices.why: Averaging throws away the assumption the gap reveals.

choices.text: Use the senior developer's card
choices.why: That is anchoring after the fact.

prompt: Planning poker is a lightweight form of Wideband ___, the method Boehm described in the 1970s.
What is the Agenda team's mean velocity over its last eight Sprints?
At the slowest velocity of the last six Sprints, 19, how many whole Sprints does a 150-point backlog take?
What forecast does the lesson give for the 150-point backlog?

choices.text: It cannot be forecast in points
choices.why: It can, from velocity.

choices.text: Exactly 6 Sprints
choices.why: A single number hides that 7 or 8 is ordinary.

choices.text: 4.8 Sprints, from the fastest Sprint
choices.why: The fastest alone is the most optimistic case.

choices.text: 5 to 8 Sprints, most likely 6
choices.why: Right. The range comes from the fastest and slowest of the last six.

prompt: Why is the 5-to-8 forecast still optimistic, by the lesson?
hint: What does it assume about the backlog?

choices.text: A fixed backlog of 150
choices.why: Right. It assumes the backlog stays at 150 points; backlogs grow, and a forecast that ignores growth runs short.

choices.text: Partly done items are not counted
choices.why: Not counting them is correct, not optimistic.

choices.text: Velocity always falls over time
choices.why: Nothing says it must fall.

choices.text: The mean of 25 is too low
choices.why: The issue is the scope, not the mean.

prompt: Match each statement to what it is.
hint: Precision is how finely; accuracy is how close.

prompt: A team cannot decide between 5 and 8 and records 7.5 points. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; it is a fair compromise
choices.why: It looks fair and adds false precision.

choices.text: Points cannot be estimated by a team
choices.why: Teams estimate points together.

choices.text: It should be rounded to 7
choices.why: 7 is not on the scale either.

choices.text: It claims a distinction the scale refuses
choices.why: Right. Pick 5 or 8, or split the story.

prompt: Which rule of thumb does the lesson give for stating a number?

choices.text: Always two decimal places
choices.why: A fixed number of decimals says nothing about knowledge.

choices.text: Round every estimate up to the next whole week of work
choices.why: Rounding up is padding, not honesty.

choices.text: No more digits than you would bet on
choices.why: Right. If you would not bet on 5.96 against 6.2, say 6, or a range.

choices.text: State the number the spreadsheet gives
choices.why: That is how the fallacy starts.

prompt: What does forecasting by counting items require of a team?

choices.text: A velocity in points
choices.why: Throughput in items replaces points.

choices.text: Every item estimated in hours first
choices.why: Counting skips sizing altogether.

choices.text: Items split to a similar small size
choices.why: Right. Items from half a day to three weeks cannot be counted usefully.

choices.text: Sprints of exactly one week
choices.why: Counting works with any cadence.

prompt: Match each approach to what its forecast uses.
What does the lesson say matters more than the choice of unit?

choices.text: Using points, because they are relative
choices.why: Points are one valid choice of three.

choices.text: Estimating every item, however small
choices.why: #NoEstimates argues the opposite.

choices.text: A range from the team's own history
choices.why: Right. Any of the three can give one; a single number from none of them is honest.

choices.text: Matching the unit the stakeholders prefer
choices.why: Preference matters less than how the forecast is built.

prompt: Team A's velocity is 40 and team B's is 25. What can be concluded about productivity?

choices.text: B estimates more carefully
choices.why: Nothing in the numbers shows care.

choices.text: A should help B
choices.why: Maybe, but not because of velocity.

choices.text: A is 60% more productive
choices.why: The units are not comparable.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Each team's points are calibrated to its own reference stories.

prompt: Management asks for velocity to rise 10% next quarter. What does the lesson predict?

choices.text: Inflated estimates, same work
choices.why: Right. It rises through bigger estimates for the same work: a measure that becomes a target stops measuring.

choices.text: Quality improves
choices.why: Nothing links the target to quality.

choices.text: Velocity cannot change on request
choices.why: It changes easily; that is the problem.

choices.text: The team works 10% faster
choices.why: Nothing about the work changes.

prompt: A developer spent the Sprint fixing an incident and unblocking others, and finished no stories. What does measuring points per person say about them, and what does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: Zero: the measure punishes vital work
choices.why: Right. It punishes the work that makes a team effective, and people learn to stop doing it.

choices.text: Nothing, since points per person are averaged out
choices.why: Points per person are not averaged; they are attributed.

choices.text: Full credit, since incidents earn points
choices.why: Incidents carry no points in the lesson's scheme.

choices.text: Zero, and they should be coached to pick up stories
choices.why: The work they did was the most valuable that Sprint.

prompt: Which of these are misuses of story points, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A team forecasting its own release from its own velocity
choices.why: That is the one legitimate use.

choices.text: Ranking teams by velocity
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Setting a velocity target
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Fixing one point as six hours
choices.why: Yes.
